title: Birthday match: how many?
blocks: How many people do you need in a room before two of them probably share a birthday? Not 183. The real answer is just 23.
Here are the rules. Ignore leap years. Every day is equally likely. And we want the chance that at least two people share a birthday.
Don't count people. Count pairs. With two people, there's one pair. Three people, three pairs. Ten people, forty-five pairs. Twenty-three people, two hundred fifty-three pairs.

Each pair has only a one in three hundred sixty-five chance to match. But there are two hundred fifty-three of them, and every pair gets a try. With 23 people, the chance passes fifty percent. With 30, seventy percent. With 50, ninety-seven percent. With 70, over ninety-nine point nine percent.

The easy way to compute it is to ask the opposite. What's the chance that everyone has a different birthday? The second person must avoid one day: three hundred sixty-four out of three hundred sixty-five. The third must avoid two days. And so on. Multiply them all, and by person twenty-three, the product drops below one half.
It feels wrong because we compare ourselves to the room: you against twenty-two others. But the room compares everyone to everyone. That's two hundred fifty-three pairs, not twenty-two.
So when a coincidence seems too big to be chance, count the pairs first. The odds you're ignoring are usually hiding in the number of chances.
